strengths: Comprehensive and convincing empirical evaluation: the paper evaluates on two major benchmarks (SUPERB and HEAR) plus fine-tuning on LibriSpeech ASR and AudioSet AT, covering understanding, paralinguistic, enhancement, environment, and music task categories.

Fair head-to-head comparisons at matched scale and pre-training data: SPEAR_s Base/Large vs. WavLM Base+/Large use essentially the same corpora and model sizes, and the speech model wins on 12/15 SUPERB tasks, lending credibility to the central claim rather than relying on scale advantages.

Interesting and well-supported finding that students can outperform their distillation teachers (e.g., BASE-AUDIO-1 outperforming ATST-frame; LARGE-H-1 outperforming HuBERT Large at equal data), which substantiates the value of the fine-grained MVQ target formulation beyond simple knowledge distillation.

Thorough ablation studies (teacher choice, number of codebooks, masked/unmasked loss balance alpha, dual-domain loss strategies, MVQ vs. k-means feature subspaces) that provide genuine insight into why the method works, e.g., the analysis that alpha=0.5 diverges from HuBERT-style masked-only prediction due to the harder fine-grained pretext task.

Honest treatment of limitations: the paper acknowledges degradation on VC, the data imbalance toward speech (only 13k/197k hours of general audio), and gaps to Dasheng 1.2B on music/environment tasks, and provides an ethics statement.

The asymmetrical dual-domain pre-training strategy (Eq. 6) is a sensible, ablated design choice, and the scaling experiment (600M XLarge on 197k hours) demonstrates the framework scales in both model and data size.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is modest: the method is essentially multi-teacher distillation recast as masked token prediction, combining existing components (MVQ from Guo et al. 2023, Zipformer encoder, WavLM/Dasheng teachers). The ablations themselves show that final performance is largely determined by teacher quality, which weakens the framing of SPEAR as a fundamentally new SSL formulation.

The claim of being 'the first unified SSL framework for speech and audio' is overstated; prior work such as SSAST (Gong et al., 2022) already pre-trained jointly on speech and audio data, and the distinction drawn in Related Work is somewhat narrow. The positioning should be softened.

Some comparisons are not strictly apples-to-apples: the XLarge model (600M params, 197k hours including Yodas-granary) is compared against WavLM Large (317M, 94k hours) when claiming new SOTA on AudioSet AT (mAP 50.0), and several baselines (BEATs, EAT) use far less data; the data-matched claim holds only for the Base/Large models.

Presentation issues in Table 6 (HEAR): the SPEAR_a rows appear twice with different scores (final-layer vs. all-layer-concatenation evaluation) without clear labeling in the main table, making the results difficult to parse and compare; similar confusion affects which numbers correspond to which evaluation protocol.

No variance reporting or statistical significance testing; given that some claimed improvements are small (e.g., 0.1 WER differences between single- and dual-domain Large models, 0.2-0.3 HEAR points), single-run results limit confidence in these fine-grained comparisons.

Reproducibility is partially deferred: only inference code and checkpoints are promised, with training details in appendices; the training code for the full pipeline (including MVQ quantizer training on teacher representations) is not stated to be released, and release is contingent on post-review updates.

strengths: Strong and comprehensive empirical evidence: the paper evaluates on both fine-tuning (LibriSpeech ASR, AudioSet AT) and frozen-representation benchmarks (SUPERB, HEAR), covering three model scales and both single-domain and dual-domain pre-training configurations. The claimed new SOTA on SUPERB (12/15 tasks vs. WavLM Large at matched model size and comparable pre-training data) is well supported by the reported tables.

The paper convincingly demonstrates that the student can exceed the teacher (e.g., SPEAR_s Large outperforms WavLM Large; LARGE-H-1 outperforms HuBERT Large with the same data), directly addressing the common criticism that KD-based approaches are teacher-bounded.

Thorough ablation studies cover teacher model choice, teacher layer, masked vs. unmasked loss weighting, encoder architecture (Zipformer vs. Transformer), MVQ vs. k-means targets, number of codebooks, loss balancing (λ), and dual-domain strategies (JOINT/DISJOINT/ASYMMETRICAL), with plausible mechanistic interpretations (e.g., UMAP analysis of codebook subspaces in Appendix F.4.2).

A controlled, teacher- and data-aligned comparison against USAD (Appendix G) strengthens the central claim that masked token prediction over MVQ targets is a better fusion interface than pure feature matching, with a clear explanation of why joint L1 matching across disparate embedding spaces is problematic.
Good reproducibility: detailed pre-training/fine-tuning hyperparameters, GPU-hours, dataset composition, and a commitment to release code and pre-trained models.

Token mixing is a sensible alternative to WavLM-style denoising that targets complex sound scenes, and the ablation (Table 6) shows clear gains on separation-oriented tasks (SD, SS, SE) at similar ASR WERs.
weaknesses: Core methodological novelty is modest: the approach combines well-established components (masked prediction of discrete units à la HuBERT, knowledge distillation from frozen SSL teachers, a Zipformer encoder, mixup-style augmentation). MVQ targets and the asymmetric dual-domain loss are incremental design choices rather than a fundamentally new framework; the ASYMMETRICAL strategy is justified mainly empirically with a post-hoc interpretation.

Heavy dependence on strong external teachers (WavLM Large, Dasheng 1.2B) means the 'unified SSL' framing is partly indirect—performance gains may largely reflect teacher quality rather than the pre-training objective per se, although the teacher-selection ablations partially mitigate this concern.

The asymmetric objective (speech tokens as universal targets, audio tokens only for audio inputs) risks embedding a speech bias into the 'unified' representation; the paper acknowledges data imbalance issues (e.g., HEAR environment/music results trail Dasheng) but the unification story is only partially validated.

Token mixing (Eqn. 4) is a frame-level stochastic target replacement that appears somewhat ad hoc; no analysis is given of why frame-level token exchange (as opposed to segment-level or waveform-level mixing of targets) is the right mechanism, and the mixing ablation is limited to Base-scale speech models on LibriSpeech.

Pre-training data is English-only speech; multilingual generalisation and generative capability (VC results degrade with scale) are unexplored, limiting the generality of the 'foundation model' framing.

Results appear to be single-run without variance estimates or significance tests; several claimed improvements (e.g., over WavLM Large on individual SUPERB tasks) are small relative to typical benchmark noise.

Minor presentation issues: loss numbering inconsistencies (references to 'Equation 4' for λ appear to point to the wrong equation), and some claims of 'state-of-the-art' should be more carefully qualified (e.g., 'pre-trained solely on AudioSet').

strengths: The paper addresses a clearly important problem—unifying speech and general-audio self-supervised representation learning—with a coherent and well-motivated framework (SPEAR) that combines multi-codebook vector quantisation targets with masked token prediction, an asymmetric dual-domain loss, and a token-mixing mechanism for complex sound scenes.

The empirical evaluation is unusually comprehensive: fine-tuning on LibriSpeech ASR and AudioSet, frozen evaluation on SUPERB (all 15+ tasks with full results in the appendix) and HEAR (19 tasks), plus scaling from Base (94M) to XLarge (600M). The claimed SOTA on SUPERB (12/15 tasks surpassing WavLM Large) and strong HEAR results are supported by detailed tables.

The ablation studies are thorough and genuinely informative: teacher model and layer selection, masked/unmasked loss weighting (α), Zipformer vs Transformer backbones, MVQ vs k-means targets (with both quantitative results and a UMAP feature-subspace analysis), number of codebooks, λ balancing, and three dual-domain training strategies. This substantially strengthens the soundness of the design choices.

A controlled, teacher- and data-aligned comparison with the closest prior work (USAD) is provided in Appendix G, which directly supports the central claim that SPEAR's masked-prediction-over-discrete-tokens objective outperforms pure feature matching; the qualitative explanation of why L1 feature matching across disparate domains is ill-defined is persuasive.

The token mixing mechanism is a sensible contribution, and the ablation (Table 6) shows it outperforms WavLM-style denoising on separation/diarisation/enhancement tasks, validating the claim that secondary signals should not be treated purely as noise.

Reproducibility is strong: hyperparameters, GPU hours, data mixtures, fine-tuning recipes, and model configurations are documented, and the authors commit to releasing code and pre-trained checkpoints. An impact statement addressing potential misuse (speaker identification, synthetic audio) is included.
weaknesses: The framework is largely a combination of existing techniques (MVQ quantisation from Guo et al. 2023, masked token prediction à la HuBERT, distillation from frozen domain teachers); the novelty is in the composition and the asymmetric dual-domain objective rather than a fundamentally new method. The token mixing is a modest, somewhat heuristic extension of mixup-style augmentation.

Heavy dependence on very strong, expensive teachers (WavLM Large, Dasheng 1.2B, itself trained on 272k hours) means some of the gains may reflect teacher quality rather than the framework; the teacher-quality ablation partially addresses this but is limited to Base scale.

The general-audio pre-training corpus is small (~13k hours, partly music datasets) compared to AudioSet-scale audio SSL, which weakens the strength of the claim that SPEAR is a general-purpose audio model; the authors themselves note HEAR performance trails Dasheng 1.2B, and the fairness of comparing SPEAR against models trained on vastly more audio data is sometimes awkward.

No variance reporting, seeds, or statistical significance tests are provided for downstream results, despite some reported margins being small (e.g., 0.1 WER gap between dual-domain and single-domain specialists).
Token mixing is applied to only 10% of samples with a limited hyperparameter exploration (SNR range, mixing probability), so the robustness of this component across settings is under-characterised.

Generation-related capabilities (VC) degrade with scale and are deferred to future work, so the 'general-purpose foundation model' framing is not fully demonstrated across both understanding and generation.
